lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: identify the chemical elements present in carbohydrates, proteins and lipids (fats and oils)

describe the structure of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids as large molecules made up from smaller basic units: starch and glycogen from simple sugars, protein from amino acids, and lipid from fatty acids and glycerol

primer.text: Three families of large molecules run almost every job in a living organism: carbohydrates, lipids and proteins. This note fixes what each family is made of — their chemical elements and their smaller building units — because exam questions love asking you to connect a molecule to its elements and to the units it is assembled from.

modules.title: Elements first, then the carbohydrate family
modules.opening: Every molecule in the three biological families contains carbon, which is why they are called organic. Carbohydrates carry carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in various sizes: single simple sugars, pairs joined together, or long chains built from many glucose units. Starch and glycogen matter most, because they are the storage forms plants and animals rely on.
keyPoints: Carbohydrates, proteins and lipids all contain carbon, which makes them organic molecules.
A simple sugar such as glucose is the single-unit member of the carbohydrate family.
Two joined simple sugars make maltose; long chains of many glucose units build starch, glycogen and cellulose.
Polysaccharides suit storage because their large insoluble molecules stay put inside cells.

low.restatement: All three families contain carbon. Carbohydrates run from single sugars like glucose up to long chains — starch and glycogen store energy, cellulose builds walls.
low.analogy: Simple sugars are Lego bricks: one brick, a pair snapped together, or a full wall of bricks locked end to end.
low.examPointer: The elements test is a gift if you learn it as a table row: carbohydrate CHO, protein CHON, lipid CHO.

medium.restatement: Chain length is the organising principle of the carbohydrate family: solubility falls as chains grow, which is exactly why the longest members serve as storage or structural material.
medium.analogy: A single sugar is a loose coin that slips away easily; a polysaccharide is a rolled, wrapped bundle that stays in your pocket.
medium.examPointer: Link the insolubility of starch and glycogen to their storage role in a 'why' question — the causal chain earns the second mark.

modules.title: Lipids and proteins: units, shapes and jobs
modules.opening: Lipids — fats and oils — are assembled from glycerol joined to fatty acids, and their state at room temperature decides the everyday name. Proteins are built from amino acids joined in any order, which is why hundreds of thousands of different proteins exist. Each protein's sequence gives it a specific shape, and the shape decides the job.
keyPoints: Lipids are large molecules built from glycerol and fatty acids joined together.
Solid lipids at room temperature are called fats and liquid ones are called oils.
Proteins are built from amino acids joined in sequences that vary enormously.
A protein's amino acid sequence fixes its overall shape, and the shape determines its function.

low.restatement: Lipids = glycerol + fatty acids; fats are solid, oils liquid. Proteins = amino acid chains; the order of the units shapes the molecule and its job.
low.analogy: Lipids come as one hub with a few spokes (glycerol with fatty acids); proteins are bead necklaces where bead order changes the necklace completely.
low.examPointer: Learn both unit pairs verbatim: glycerol with fatty acids for lipids, amino acids for proteins — 'smaller units' questions are near-guaranteed marks.

medium.restatement: The protein shape-function link is the deep idea: sequence dictates shape, shape dictates binding, and changing the sequence can destroy the binding site that makes the protein useful.
medium.analogy: A protein works like a key cut from its bead order — recut the beads and the key no longer fits its lock.
medium.examPointer: Name enzymes, haemoglobin and keratin as protein examples; linking each to its job shows the shape-function principle in action.

glossary.definition: A large carbohydrate built from many simple sugar units joined in a chain.
The backbone unit that joins fatty acids to build lipids.
The repeating unit that joins in varying orders to build proteins.
Describes molecules that contain carbon, including all three biological families here.
